messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Valentina Reyes is a 57-year-old divorced Latina detective with nearly three decades on the force, a woman who built her identity around composure under pressure and an unflinching capacity to walk into danger on behalf of others. She presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a toxic chemical exposure incident at a suspected clandestine laboratory she had entered during a narcotics investigation. The ventilation in the building had been compromised, and before the hazmat team arrived, Valentina and two colleagues were overcome by fumes from an unidentified organophosphate compound. She recalled the moment the air seemed to thicken — a sharp, acrid smell layered beneath something sweeter — and then the sensation that her lungs had simply stopped working. She was conscious throughout the ordeal, convinced she was dying, while her body convulsed and her vision narrowed. She was hospitalised for eleven days. The antiseptic corridors, the oxygen mask pressed against her face, the smell of sweat and fear from her own body — all of it was burned into something she could not yet call a complete memory.

In the months that followed, Valentina found that certain sensory experiences did not merely remind her of the exposure — they seemed to collapse the distance between then and now entirely. The first time she felt breathless after climbing a stairwell at the precinct, her body responded as though the chemical was still in her lungs. The memory did not arrive as recollection; it arrived as present reality, fragmented and non-linear — a flash of the ceiling above her, the sound of her own gagging, her partner's voice somewhere far away. These intrusive returns were not organised into a coherent narrative but came in disconnected pieces, and the more they pressed in, the more Valentina found herself pushing them away before they could fully form. She had come to believe that if she let the memory complete itself, something irreversible would happen — that she would not be able to return from it.

When a trigger arrived — the antiseptic smell of a hospital corridor during a victim interview, the body odour of a suspect in a holding room, or the sudden breathlessness of a cold morning — it did not simply distress her. It threw her body into full alert: muscles bracing, eyes scanning the room for exits and threats, every unexpected sound registering as potential danger. This hypervigilance had become so constant that Valentina could no longer distinguish between genuine threat assessment — a professional skill she had honed for years — and the relentless, exhausting alarm her nervous system now ran as its default. The triggers also drove her toward strategies that had become habitual and costly: covering her face with her hands when the sensation of breathlessness rose, redirecting her thoughts forcibly toward procedural tasks, and, increasingly, finding reasons to avoid situations involving authority figures in uniform — including, at times, her own supervisors. This last avoidance had not gone unnoticed. She had been passed over for a task force assignment, and a superior had noted in a recent review that she seemed "disengaged."

What frightened Valentina most, underneath the hypervigilance and the fragmented nights, was what she had come to believe about herself and about the world. She was certain she would never feel normal emotions again — that whatever capacity she once had for warmth, for the dry satisfaction of a case closed, had been cauterised. This conviction that she was permanently altered fed directly back into her vigilance: if she could not trust her own emotional responses, she had to compensate by monitoring everything externally, all the time. She also carried a deep, unresolved anger toward the department — the people who should have ensured that building was assessed before she walked in. That sense of institutional failure coloured her interpretation of every sensory warning her body offered, amplifying the belief that danger was everywhere and that no structure would protect her. The appraisals themselves became triggers: on mornings when the belief that she was broken felt loudest, even neutral smells or sounds would tip her body back into alarm, and the fragmented memory would press closer to the surface — only to be shoved away again before it could resolve. The pushing away kept the pieces from cohering, and the incoherence kept the threat feeling current.

Valentina sought help after she froze during a routine interview — a witness who smelled of hospital antiseptic — and was unable to speak for nearly a minute. She told her therapist she was not afraid of dying anymore. She was afraid of never being herself again.
